answers.speaker: A
answers.reply: According to the East Hollow committee's September 2019 memorandum, signed by Rina Vale, the rule for who may use the temporary storm-access tokens is register-based: thirty households appear on the register, ten from each of three lanes. A token permits a household to use the staffed service crossing during its assigned morning window. The record states two express exclusions: the token neither reserves a vehicle nor grants permission to enter the closed bridge, and a household may not hand its token to another household. Goods carried by an admitted group receive no separate priority. The required record check is performed at the crossing: a steward checks both the lane identifier and the issue date carried on the token before admitting a group. Two marks document the relevant events but at different stages: the clerk places a triangular mark on a token at the moment of issue, and the attendant adds a short horizontal stroke only after admitting the household. The memorandum's stated limits on the check are: (1) a triangle alone is not evidence that anyone actually crossed; (2) in the retrospective check, the committee selected twelve issued tokens, of which nine had corresponding entries in the crossing ledger and three did not, and the memorandum leaves both unused tokens and incomplete ledger pages as possible explanations for the unmatched cases; (3) it reports no investigation of individual households and assigns no penalty for an unmatched entry alone; and (4) the check cannot establish how often people crossed without a token or whether the arrangement shortened average waiting times. The author concludes only that the marks can distinguish issue from admission when both records survive. The record also states one time-limited exception: if the service crossing closes before a household's window ends, the token can be moved to the following morning once, and the clerk must first confirm the closure with the attendant. A worked example adds that a household arriving in the afternoon instead of its morning window simply joins the ordinary queue, and the attendant does not erase and replace the token's window; the memorandum presents this as explaining how the recorded scheduling rule was applied, not as prescribing a response to every possible emergency.

Two further conditions appear in the record: a holder could not pass the permission to another household, and the token gave no special entitlement for carried goods.

The required record check is a two-inscription reading of each token: one must distinguish the office's circular issue stamp from the attendant's vertical admission line. Only the vertical admission line records that the group was actually admitted; a circular stamp by itself cannot establish a crossing. The office separately recorded an issue day alongside the group identifier. The check Doren describes was staff comparing fifteen temporary tokens with admission sheets, finding a corresponding entry for eleven of them, which left four unmatched records.

The stated limits of that check are as follows. The four unmatched records are presented as a puzzle, not a claim of misconduct: for any of the four, either the token remained unused or its admission sheet went missing, and the note does not settle which explanation applies to any case. The staff made no household-by-household inquiry, and unmatched paperwork alone incurred no sanction. Doren expressly cautions against using this small check to calculate total unauthorized crossings. Surviving pairs of records can show the distinction between issuance and admission, but they do not demonstrate a reduction in waiting time or the completeness of every day's sheets.

On time limits and exceptions, the record states that an afternoon closure could justify a single extension to the next afternoon, but only after the attendant confirmed that service had stopped. In the described late-arrival case, a family that appeared the following morning was placed in the ordinary queue instead of having its afternoon allocation rewritten.
